title: Effect of water running and cycling on maximum oxygen consumption and 2-mile run performance
authors: Eyestone ED, Fellingham G, George J, Fisher AG
journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
population: 32 trained subjects aged 18 to 26 (the abstract gives no sex split), not described as injured, stratified by 2-mile run pretest into high, medium and low performance levels
findings: Thirty-two trained subjects aged 18 to 26 were stratified by a 2-mile run pretest and randomly assigned to water running, cycling or running training, with similar frequency, duration and intensity over 6 weeks (abstract).

After 6 weeks all groups made a small but statistically significant decrease in VO2max but no change in 2-mile run time, with no difference by training modality or pretraining performance level (abstract).

The authors conclude that over 6 weeks, runners who cannot run because of soft tissue injury can maintain VO2max and 2-mile run performance similar to running training with either cycling or water running (abstract).
limitations: Abstract only (closed access). Trained subjects aged 18 to 26, not described as injured, and not injured runners: the conclusion about injured runners is the authors' extrapolation. Small groups, 6 weeks, a 2-mile run, nobody over 26 and no distance beyond 2 miles, no injury or return-to-running outcome. All groups lost a little VO2max, so the result is of maintenance with a small loss, not of no change.
implications: Supports a statement that, over about 6 weeks in young trained adults, cycling or water running at the same frequency, duration and intensity kept 2-mile run time as running did, with a small fall in VO2max in every group.

Does not support any rate at which cycling or pool work counts toward run load, the effect of a niggle or of cross-training on tissue capacity, or a benefit for older or less trained runners or for runs of a half marathon or longer.
